name: Gareth Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, government, unions and AI companies. This is confidential. Gareth, what is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We take the permit from the depot, drive out with the right crossarm if stores has done its job, isolate the line and repair the damaged section. I like working beside a newer lineworker and seeing him make a safe check without being prompted. The tiring part is explaining a delayed repair when the part or the map was wrong.

say: I would say a **tidier permit** helps, while line repairs remain hands-on.
I would keep a **paper isolation copy** at the job site.
think: I do not use **AI tools** and expect my repair work to continue.
Our **three-month cushion** and regular wage make a missed standby payment manageable.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** and mentor the newer worker on isolation.
Check the **printed permit** against the job number before departure.
feel: I feel **settled** about work and the household budget.
S0.quote: The paper permit let us check the isolation number while dispatch restored the link.
fieldNote: Gareth values **paper isolation records** after a real signal loss at a creek crossing, and he has never used AI.
His **three-month cushion** and typical wage support a calm response even with a mortgage and school-age children.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and mentor the newer worker on isolation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a tidy permit is pleasant, but the outage still ends when we fix the conductor. I have worked long enough to keep the paper isolation copy in my jacket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI, and a small filing change would not alter my job much. We have about three months of expenses saved, the mortgage is manageable on my regular wage and there are a few line employers within a drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the repair rota and keep mentoring the newer worker on safe isolation. In the first year I would check each printed permit against the job number before the van leaves, as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled. My family still watches the budget, but one delayed standby payment would not put the mortgage in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you keep the paper copy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the creek crossing last spring the tablet lost its signal after the crew parked. The paper permit let us check the isolation number while dispatch restored the link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the small AI change affect your colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The permit clerk might spend less time copying numbers, but I would expect the job to remain. I would ask her what the change actually removes before making a claim for the whole depot.

say: I would argue that **crew size** should follow site safety, not a faster office plan.
I would ask the **safety committee** to review real repairs before targets change.
think: I expect **office job cuts** first and worry about faulty orders reaching our crew.
My own **regular wage** seems stable enough to raise the issue early.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and bring a staffing rule to the next union meeting.
Log **wrong parts** and time estimates for a group meeting with management.
feel: I feel **wary for colleagues** and annoyed by computer-set climb times.
S1.quote: A single complaint can sound personal, while three notebooks show a pattern.
fieldNote: Gareth sees **office automation** as a safety issue that can reach field crews through parts and time targets.
His **steady income and savings** let him act through the union before he expects personal wage loss.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the scheduling change
Bring a crew-size proposal and wrong-order log to the union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that buying software must not turn a three-person repair into a two-person instruction. The line needs a safe crew even if an office plan is produced in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and scheduling staff may be cut before our line crews are. I do not expect to lose my job soon, but a leaner office could send the wrong crossarm and leave us waiting on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my shifts and bring a proposed staffing rule to the next union meeting. During the first year of new scheduling I would write down incorrect parts and unsafe time estimates, then present the log with two colleagues to the depot manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary for the office staff and annoyed by the idea of a computer setting climb times. My own wage looks stable for now, so I can afford to speak up before a bad rule settles in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staffing rule say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would keep at least the current crew size for a live-line repair until the safety committee reviews actual jobs. I would use the creek crossing job to show why a screen cannot see every hazard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring two colleagues to management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A single complaint can sound personal, while three notebooks show a pattern. I would want the union representative present so the meeting is recorded.

say: I would distinguish **2028 office AI** from line robots around 2031.
I would demand a **written robot trial rule** before live-line work.
think: I will be **48** when robots arrive, and three months saved would not replace years of wages.
A few **nearby line employers** might offer work, but their vacancies are uncertain.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** after 2028 and attend union bargaining talks.
Apply for a **nearby line vacancy** if our own rota begins to shrink.
feel: I feel **worried but capable** of acting with savings and other employers nearby.
S2.quote: A robot trial labelled supervised is too thin for the crew without named safety roles.
fieldNote: Gareth separates the **three-year robot lag** from immediate office automation and expects paid repairs at first.
His **moderate cushion** provides time to bargain, but he treats nearby vacancies and paid training as conditional.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts in the first 2028 AI year
Attend union bargaining talks on robot staffing and trial liability
Apply for a nearby posted line job if his rota shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 can rewrite the office plan, but line-capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the union to seek a written trial rule before a machine touches a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 for the office change and 48 for the robot change. Three months of savings gives us breathing room, but it would not carry the mortgage for years if field crews were reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union branch to put robot staffing and paid retraining on the next bargaining agenda. In the first year after 2028 I would keep the repair shifts, attend the talks and apply for a posted line post at another nearby electricity company if our own rota began to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried but not without choices. There are a few nearby line employers, though I cannot assume they will be hiring when robots reach all of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a trial rule need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should name who isolates the line, who inspects the robot-made joint and who carries liability if the joint fails. A robot trial labelled supervised is too thin for the crew without named safety roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a course in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the company paid the hours and showed a real field role at the end. I am slow with unfamiliar screens and would not leave steady wages for a training promise.

say: I would ask for **recorded field trials** before staffing talks.
I would explain **2031 thinking AI** precedes hands-on robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still owe on the mortgage and need wages.
A **report-only inspection job** could disappear under full AI.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2031 and review field trial records with the union.
Consider a **paid practical course** only if linked to a posted field role.
feel: I feel **watchful**, with time and a savings cushion to assess evidence.
S3.quote: I would want a signed job description with site visits, not just report checking.
fieldNote: Gareth uses his **moderate savings** to seek trial evidence and negotiated terms before personally changing work.
He knows full AI can take **report checking**, so a field inspection offer must include site visits and pay.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts through the first 2031 AI year
Review robot field trial records with the union safety committee
Take a company-paid practical inspection course if linked to a posted role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets the union bargain from evidence rather than a rumour. Full thinking AI comes by 2031, while robots capable of field repairs follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the first date and 51 at the robot date. Our older child may have left school, but we could still owe on the mortgage and I cannot assume a pension at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the safety committee to record the results of every robot field trial. In 2031 I would keep my line shifts, review the trial record with the union and consider a company-paid practical inspection course if it led to a posted role at similar pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than frightened. A five-year warning and our savings give us time to see what works, although I will not call the field job permanent after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection role real to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a signed job description with site visits, not just report checking. Full AI could write the reports, so paper work alone would not protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another depot before 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the local hours dropped and another company posted a comparable line job. I know the routes here, and moving early for a rumour would cost my family stability.

say: I would seek **yearly crew-hour reports** and robot fault records.
I would distinguish **2036 office AI** from field robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still owe on the mortgage and have no retirement plan confirmed.
A **site inspection post** could matter if field hours eventually fall.
do: Keep paid **field repairs** and review annual figures with union colleagues.
In **2036**, apply for site inspection if my hours fall and a post is advertised.
feel: I feel **steady for now** and cautious about future field staffing.
S4.quote: A glossy robot trial report without paid crew hours or bad-weather repair checks would not help my family plan.
fieldNote: Gareth expects **paid hands-on work** through the near term, using union review rather than a rushed move.
He keeps an existing **savings cushion** intact and does not mistake it for newly saving or a funded retirement.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the first 2036 AI year
Review yearly crew-hour and robot fault reports with union colleagues
Apply for an advertised site inspection role if his hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot a decade is long enough for proper bargaining and a proper safety record. Full thinking AI arrives in 2036, and robots able to repair lines around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the office changes and 56 at the robot date. The children should be adults, but the mortgage might still be there; I have not checked whether retirement at 56 would be possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stay on repairs and ask for yearly reports of crew hours and robot faults. In 2036 I would keep the paid field rota, compare the reports with union colleagues and apply for a posted inspection role if my own hours were falling and the role involved site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the next few years. I can work, watch the figures and make a choice later, though I would not tell a new apprentice that line work is certain forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay down the mortgage faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already make regular payments and have a few months saved. I would keep that cushion rather than empty it just because a possible robot date is on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many paid crew hours remain and who checks robot repairs in bad weather. A glossy robot trial report without paid crew hours or bad-weather repair checks would not help my family plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The three-year gap before field robots arrive is short if the company moves without trial rules. Written safety and staffing terms, paid practical training tied to a field role, and honest crew-hour figures would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who carries responsibility when a robot-made joint fails in a storm. A worker should not be blamed for a machine repair the company chose to send out.

headlineQuote: A worker should not be blamed for a machine repair the company chose to send out.
portrait: Gareth is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
His **three-month savings cushion**, typical pay and some nearby line employers give him choices the fastest scenario still tests.
He has **never used AI** and trusts paper permits, field evidence and familiar safety routines.
Across the scenarios he seeks **union terms** and real robot trial records before considering paid training or another field post.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves only three years before robots could reach his field work without agreed safety rules.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing and safety terms**, paid practical training and honest crew-hour figures would help him decide.
